Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Research Letter Serologic Evidence of Avian Influenza Virus Exposure in Livestock, Egypt, 2024–2026 Suggested citation for this article Abstract Spillover of influenza A(H5N1) virus to cattle in the United States sparked global concern. We investigated whether endemic avian influenza viruses are potentially spilling over into domestic livestock in Egypt. We detected influenza H9N2 antibodies in 2.5% and H5N1 antibodies in 2.9%–4.5% of tested animals. Additional surveillance will elucidate host infection dynamics. The emergence of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b virus in dairy cattle in the United States represented a major shift in influenza virus ecology, marking the first sustained transmission of H5N1 virus in a mammalian livestock species (1). Genotype B3.13 was reported in dairy cows in early 2024 in several US states; data indicated a spillover event from wild birds to cattle and then interstate transmission through cow movement (1). A defining feature of H5N1 virus infection in dairy cattle is its marked tropism for the mammary gland, resulting in extremely high viral titers in milk and relatively lower viral loads in respiratory samples (2). Mechanical transmission via the milking process is believed to play a major role in cow-to-cow transmission, particularly in large dairy operations. Cow infection was not limited to genotype B3.13; European genotype euDG was shown to be able to cause infection in an experimental setting (3), and North American genotype D1.1 was detected in cattle in the United States (3). Infection of other livestock species, including goats, sheep, swine, and alpacas, was reported in mixed-species backyards and farms in the United States and United Kingdom (4,5). In 2026, a farm in the Netherlands had a cat infected with H5N1 virus; a cow at that farm had antibodies against the virus (6). Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus and low-pathogenicity avian influenza A(H9N2) virus are widely and endemically circulating in poultry in Egypt on farms and backyards and at live bird markets (7). Subtype H5N1 was detected in feral rats in poultry production areas (8). In addition, reassortment events between the H5N1 and H9N2 subtypes led to the emergence of novel clade 2.3.4.4b influenza A(H5N2) viruses (9). To determine whether those viruses are spilling over to livestock in Egypt, particularly in mixed-species settings, we conducted a serosurveillance study in northern Egypt. During October 2024–January 2026, we collected 444 serum samples from 33 conveniently selected small farms (≈10 cattle, no mixed species) and backyards housing cattle (1–3 cattle with mixed species) in 3 governorates (n = 155, n = 59, and n = 230) in northern Egypt, representing common practices in Egypt. Sheep and goats were also sampled if housed in the same backyards as cattle. All sampled animals were apparently healthy adults. We tested serum samples for antibodies against a 2025 Egyptian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 (A/duck/Egypt/BA20361C/2022) virus using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and microneutralization (MN) assays and against a G1-like Egypt influenza A(H9N2) (A/chicken/Egypt/RA20191OP/2022) virus by HI in accordance with World Health Organization protocols (10). We considered an antibody titer >1:40 as positive for both assays. Data on the number of cows, presence of other mammals (e.g., donkeys and horses), and presence of avian species (poultry and/or wild birds) were available for 271 samples. We performed statistical comparisons with χ2 or Fisher exact tests; we considered p<0.05 statistically significant. Overall, 11 (2.5%) serum specimens tested positive for influenza A(H9N2) antibodies, 20 (4.5%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by HI, and 13 (2.9%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by MN (Figure, panel A). Positive titers were 40–160 (Figure, panel B). None of the samples tested positive for antibodies against both viruses. Of the 20 H5N1 virus specimens positive by HI, 12 tested positive by MN; 1 specimen was negative by HI and positive by MN. All influenza H9N2-positive specimens were from 3 locations in the same governorate (p = 0.005). Influenza A(H5N1) antibodies were detected in 2 governorates; the differences in detection rates by governorate were statistically significant (0%, 1.3%, and 4.8%; p = 0.049). All H5N1 virus–seropositive specimens were from cattle (Table). We detected H9N2 antibodies in 6/374 (1.6%) of cattle specimens, 1/31 (3.2%) of goat specimens, and 4/39 (10.3%) of sheep specimens (p = 0.004). Presence of other animals did not predict seropositivity. Small farms had a significantly higher proportion of H5N1 virus–positive animals tested by MN (p = 0.039). Our findings indicate that spillover of avian influenza viruses to cattle and other livestock is not geographically restricted or caused by certain genotypes of H5N1 virus. Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus of the EA-2021-AB genotype and G1-like H9N2 virus appear to be spilling over into livestock in Egypt; however, because our evidence is serologic, we could not ascertain whether true infection is occurring and whether the same signs seen in the United States are common in cattle in Egypt. Even so, the evidence is a strong indicator that spillover is occurring, similar to that reported in Europe (4,6). Furthermore, spillover is not restricted to cattle; some sheep and goats tested in our study were seropositive for influenza A(H9N2) virus. Surveillance for avian influenza viruses in Egypt and other countries, especially those in which avian influenza is endemic, will verify infection and provide data on frequency, routes of transmission, and factors affecting infection of and transmission to livestock. Dr. Gomaa is a virologist at the National Research Centre, Giza, and a member of the Center of Scientific Excellence for virus research. His work focuses on emerging and reemerging viruses, avian influenza, coronaviruses, vaccine development, viral immunology, and pandemic preparedness. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate whether endemic avian influenza viruses are spilling over into domestic livestock in Egypt, following global concern over the spillover of influenza A(H5N1) virus to cattle in the United States.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A serosurveillance study was conducted in northern Egypt from October 2024 to January 2026, collecting 444 serum samples from 33 small farms and backyards across three governorates, representing common livestock practices in Egypt.
analysis.methods: To determine whether avian influenza viruses are spilling over to livestock in Egypt, the researchers conducted a serosurveillance study in northern Egypt, collecting serum samples from cattle in small farms and backyards.
analysis.main_results: Influenza H9N2 antibodies were detected in 2.5% of tested animals, while H5N1 antibodies were found in 2.9%–4.5% of the animals.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that avian influenza viruses may be spilling over into livestock in Egypt, highlighting the need for further surveillance to understand host infection dynamics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results inform the importance of monitoring avian influenza virus exposure in livestock to better understand transmission patterns and potential zoonotic risks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to small farms and backyards with no mixed species, and the evidence is based on serologic detection, which may not fully capture the extent of viral transmission.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the spillover of avian influenza viruses into domestic livestock in Egypt. Researchers conducted a serosurveillance study in northern Egypt from October 2024 to January 2026, collecting serum samples from 33 small farms and backyards across three governorates. They detected H9N2 antibodies in 2.5% of tested animals and H5N1 antibodies in 2.9%–4.5% of the animals. These findings suggest that avian influenza viruses may be spilling over into livestock in Egypt, emphasizing the need for additional surveillance to understand host infection dynamics. The study was limited to small farms and backyards with no mixed species, and the evidence is based on serologic detection, which may not fully capture the extent of viral transmission. The results have implications for monitoring avian influenza virus exposure in livestock to better understand transmission patterns and potential zoonotic risks.

elements_zh.methods: 为了确定 禽流感 病毒是否蔓延到埃及的牲畜身上,研究人员在埃及北部进行了一项血清监测研究,从小型农场和后院的牛身上收集了血清样本。
elements_zh.main_results: 2.5%的测试动物检测到H9N2流感抗体,2.9%–4.5%的动物检测到H5N1流感抗体。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,禽流感 病毒可能正在扩散到埃及的牲畜中,这凸显了需要进一步使用 监测 来了解 宿主 感染动态。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 结果表明监测牲畜中 禽流感 病毒暴露的重要性,以更好地了解 传播 模式和潜在的人畜共患病风险。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于没有混合物种的小农场和后院,证据基于血清学检测,可能无法完全掌握病毒 传播 的范围。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate whether endemic avian influenza viruses are spilling over into domestic livestock in Egypt, following global concern over the spillover of influenza A(H5N1) virus to cattle in the United States.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: A serosurveillance study was conducted in northern Egypt from October 2024 to January 2026, collecting 444 serum samples from 33 small farms and backyards across three governorates, representing common livestock practices in Egypt.
analysis_en.methods: To determine whether avian influenza viruses are spilling over to livestock in Egypt, the researchers conducted a serosurveillance study in northern Egypt, collecting serum samples from cattle in small farms and backyards.
analysis_en.main_results: Influenza H9N2 antibodies were detected in 2.5% of tested animals, while H5N1 antibodies were found in 2.9%–4.5% of the animals.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that avian influenza viruses may be spilling over into livestock in Egypt, highlighting the need for further surveillance to understand host infection dynamics.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results inform the importance of monitoring avian influenza virus exposure in livestock to better understand transmission patterns and potential zoonotic risks.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to small farms and backyards with no mixed species, and the evidence is based on serologic detection, which may not fully capture the extent of viral transmission.

full_text: Disclaimer: Early release articles are not considered as final versions. Any changes will be reflected in the online version in the month the article is officially released. Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Research Letter Cross-Protection against Influenza A(H5) Clade 2.3.4.4b Viruses after A(H1N1)pdm09 Infection Suggested citation for this article Abstract We challenged ferrets previously infected with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus with H5N1 or H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses to assess cross-protection. Results show that previous A(H1N1)pdm09 virus immunity conferred partial protection against both viruses, with slightly reduced protection against H5N5 compared with H5N1, potentially reflecting the absence of cross-reactive N5 neuraminidase antibodies. Influenza A(H5) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have spread widely among wild birds and poultry and caused infections in mammals, including humans, raising public health concerns (1). A case of human infection with H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b virus was reported in Washington, USA during 2025; the patient subsequently died, representing the second fatal A(H5) case in the United States (1,2). A(H1) and A(H5) hemagglutinins (HAs) belong to influenza A virus phylogenetic group 1. Most antibodies targeting the HA stalk, a conserved, membrane-proximal region of HA, are cross-reactive with HAs within the same phylogenetic group (3). Studies have demonstrated that previous influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus infection can provide some protection against H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses (4,5). The emergence of H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b virus raises questions about whether previous A(H1N1)pdm09 immunity confers similar protection against A(H5) viruses bearing antigenically distinct neuraminidases (NAs). We used a preimmune ferret model to compare cross-protection conferred by previous A(H1N1)pdm09 infection against A(H5) viruses with homologous or heterologous NA subtypes. We conducted all experiments with H5N5 and H5N1 viruses in a Biosafety Level 3 enhanced facility with approval from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. We intranasally inoculated 12 ferrets serologically naive to seasonal influenza viruses with 103 PFUs of A(H1N1)pdm09 A/Nebraska/14/2019 virus. We confirmed seroconversion 3 months postinfection by using a hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) assay, which detects antibodies that inhibit HA-mediated hemagglutination, with a geometric mean titer of 320 (95% CI 245.3–417.3) (Appendix Figure, panel A). Using previously described multiplex binding assays (6), we detected high levels of antibodies binding to the head of A(H1N1)pdm09, but not HA head or ectodomain from H5N1 or H5N5 viruses, and antibodies binding to N1 NAs from A(H1N1)pdm09 and H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses, but not N5 NA from H5N5 virus. In addition, we detected antibodies binding to the group 1 HA stalk derived from A(H1N1)pdm09 virus (Appendix Figure, panels B, C). We then intranasally challenged those animals, referred to as preimmune ferrets, with 104 PFU of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b A/Washington/239/2024 or H5N5 A/Washington/2148/2025 virus (6 ferrets per virus), alongside naive control groups without previous influenza immunity. We euthanized 3 ferrets per group on day 4 postinfection to assess viral dissemination; we monitored the remaining animals for clinical signs, weight loss, viral shedding in nasal washes, and virus presence in throat and rectal swabs. Severe disease, characterized by lethargy, fever, and substantial weight loss (maximum 13.8% in H5N1 virus inoculated ferrets and 18.4% in H5N5 virus inoculated ferrets), developed in naive ferrets inoculated with H5N1 or H5N5 viruses. We euthanized all animals on postinfection days 5–6 for H5N1 virus–inoculated ferrets and days 6–10 for H5N5 virus–inoculated ferrets after they reached predefined humane endpoints, consistent with previous reports (7,8). In contrast, preimmune ferrets challenged with H5N1 virus exhibited minimal disease, a mean maximum weight loss of 2.4%, and 100% survival (Figure 1, panels A–C). Preimmune ferrets challenged with H5N5 also showed reduced disease severity (mean maximum weight loss 7.6%); however, 1 animal reached a humane endpoint on day 7 postinfection (Figure 1, panels B, C). Preimmune ferrets challenged with either H5N1 or H5N5 virus shed similar levels of virus in nasal wash samples during days 1–4 postinfection (range of mean peak titers 103.8–105.2 PFU/mL) as naive controls but exhibited reduced titers in throat swab samples on day 4 for H5N5 virus and days 2 and 3 for H5N1 virus (Figure 2, panels A, B). Viral clearance from nasal washes occurred 2–4 days earlier in preimmune ferrets. We detected H5N1 virus less frequently in rectal swab samples from preimmune animals than from naive controls, whereas we did not observe that reduction for ferrets infected with H5N5 virus (Figure 2, panels A, B). Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus preimmunity did not substantially reduce viral titers in the upper respiratory tract (nasal turbinates) or soft palate after H5N1 or H5N5 virus challenge (Figure 2, panels C, D). However, A(H1N1)pdm09 preimmunity largely prevented viral dissemination to the lower respiratory tract (trachea and lungs) and extrapulmonary tissues for both viruses, with only sporadic low-level viral detection. However, intestinal viral titers were comparable between preimmune and naive ferrets challenged with H5N5 virus (Figure 2, panels C, D). Detection of group 1 HA stalk antibodies after A(H1N1)pdm09 infection (Appendix Figure), together with previous evidence of HA stalk-mediated cross-protection against disease caused by the influenza A viruses within the same phylogenetic group (3,9), suggests that cross-reactive HA stalk antibodies might contribute to protection against A(H5) viruses. In addition, N1 cross-reactivity might further enhance protection against H5N1 virus. Consistent with our findings, limited N5 cross-reactivity has been reported in humans despite detectable N1 responses (10). Further studies using H5-specific HA stalk antigens and functional assays are needed to determine the contribution of cross-reactive antibodies and cellular immunity to protection against zoonotic influenza A viruses. Our findings showed that previous A(H1N1)pdm09 viral infection conferred partial cross-protection against H5N1 and H5N5 viruses in ferrets, reducing disease severity, lethality, and viral dissemination. Dr. Sun is a microbiologist in the Influenza Division, National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlanta, Georgia, USA. Her research primarily focuses on using the ferret model to understand influenza virus pathogenicity and transmissibility. title_original: Cross-Protection against Influenza A(H5) Clade 2.3.4.4b Viruses after A(H1N1)pdm09 Infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess whether prior infection with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus provides cross-protection against H5N1 and H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses, which have raised public health concerns due to their spread among wild birds and poultry and their ability to infect mammals, including humans.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a preimmune ferret model to compare cross-protection conferred by previous A(H1N1)pdm09 infection against A(H5) viruses with homologous or heterologous NA subtypes. Twelve ferrets serologically naive to seasonal influenza viruses were inoculated with A(H1N1)pdm09 virus, and then challenged with H5N1 or H5N5 viruses. Naive control groups without prior influenza immunity were also included.
analysis.methods: The researchers conducted experiments in a Biosafety Level 3 enhanced facility using a hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) assay to confirm seroconversion 3 months postinfection. They also used multiplex binding assays to detect antibodies binding to HA head and stalk regions and N1/N5 neuraminidases. Ferrets were challenged with H5N1 or H5N5 viruses and monitored for clinical signs, weight loss, viral shedding, and virus presence in throat and rectal swabs.
analysis.main_results: Results showed that previous A(H1N1)pdm09 infection conferred partial protection against H5N1 and H5N5 viruses, reducing disease severity, lethality, and viral dissemination. Preimmune ferrets challenged with H5N1 exhibited minimal disease, a mean maximum weight loss of 2.4%, and 100% survival, while those challenged with H5N5 had a mean maximum weight loss of 7.6% and one animal reached a humane endpoint on day 7 postinfection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that prior A(H1N1)pdm09 immunity may provide some cross-protection against H5N1 and H5N5 viruses, potentially due to cross-reactive N1 neuraminidase antibodies, which contrasts with the absence of cross-reactive N5 neuraminidase antibodies observed in humans.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that immunity from A(H1N1)pdm09 infection might offer partial protection against H5N1 and H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in ferrets, which could inform surveillance and risk assessment strategies for avian influenza viruses in mammals, including humans.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its use of a ferret model, which may not fully represent human immune responses, and the small sample size of 6 ferrets per virus group. The evidence is moderate, as the results are based on animal models and not directly on human clinical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated whether prior infection with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus provides cross-protection against H5N1 and H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses. Using a ferret model, researchers found that previous A(H1N1)pdm09 immunity conferred partial protection, reducing disease severity and viral dissemination. However, the protection was slightly less effective against H5N5 compared to H5N1, possibly due to the absence of cross-reactive N5 neuraminidase antibodies. The findings suggest that immunity from A(H1N1)pdm09 might offer some cross-protection against H5N1 and H5N5 viruses, which could have implications for surveillance and risk assessment. The study is limited by its use of an animal model and small sample size, resulting in moderate confidence in the evidence.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估既往感染甲型(H1N1)pdm09 流感病毒是否能提供针对 H5N1 和 H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b 病毒的交叉保护,这些病毒由于在 野生鸟类 和家禽中传播以及感染包括人类在内的哺乳动物的能力而引起了公共卫生担忧。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用免疫前雪貂模型来比较先前 A(H1N1)pdm09 感染对具有同源或异源 NA 亚型的 A(H5) 病毒的交叉保护。将 12 只对季节性流感病毒进行血清学检测的雪貂接种 A(H1N1)pdm09 病毒,然后用 H5N1 或 H5N5 病毒进行攻击。还包括先前没有流感免疫力的初始对照组。
elements_zh.methods: 研究人员在生物安全 3 级增强设施中使用血凝抑制 (HAI) 测定进行了实验,以确认感染后 3 个月的血清转化。他们还使用多重结合测定来检测与 HA 头部和茎部区域以及 N1/N5 神经氨酸酶结合的抗体。雪貂接受 H5N1 或 H5N5 病毒攻击,并监测临床症状、体重减轻、病毒脱落以及喉咙和直肠拭子中病毒的存在情况。
elements_zh.main_results: 结果显示,先前的 A(H1N1)pdm09 感染可对 H5N1 和 H5N5 病毒提供部分保护,从而降低疾病的严重程度、致死率和病毒传播。接受 H5N1 攻击的免疫前雪貂表现出最小的疾病,平均最大体重减轻 2.4%,存活率为 100%,而接受 H5N5 攻击的免疫前雪貂的平均最大体重减轻为 7.6%,一只动物在感染后第 7 天达到人道终点。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,先前的 A(H1N1)pdm09 免疫力可能会针对 H5N1 和 H5N5 病毒提供一些交叉保护,这可能是由于交叉反应性 N1 神经氨酸酶抗体所致,这与在人类中观察到的交叉反应性 N5 神经氨酸酶抗体的缺失形成鲜明对比。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,A(H1N1)pdm09 感染的免疫力可能对雪貂中的 H5N1 和 H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b 病毒提供部分保护,这可以为包括人类在内的哺乳动物中的 监测 病毒和 禽流感 病毒的风险评估策略提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到雪貂模型使用的限制,该模型可能无法完全代表人类 免疫应答,而且样本量较小,每个病毒组有 6 只雪貂。证据是中等的,因为结果是基于动物模型而不是直接基于人类临床数据。
